Vulnerable cordova-plugin-inappbrowser (CVE-2026-47430) on managed iOS / mobile assets AIWeaponization High
Hunts for managed devices reporting CVE-2026-47430 — vulnerable versions (3.1.0 through 6.0.0) of the iOS cordova-plugin-inappbrowser shipped inside in-house or third-party Cordova/Ionic mobile apps. This is an asset-prioritisation hunt; the article is a disclosure advisory with no IOCs, in-the-wild payload, or attacker infrastructure that endpoint/SIEM telemetry could match on. Rationale: Article gives exact affected range (3.1.0–6.0.0), exact fixed version (6.0.1), and CVE-2026-47430. No IOCs, no in-the-wild payloads, no attacker infrastructure exist — so a behavioural endpoint/network detection would be a fabricated template. The honest detection is asset discovery: surface managed iOS devices carrying the vulnerable package so they can be prioritised for patching. TVM tables are the right pivot because they're the only place embedded library CVEs surface in M365 Defender / Sentinel. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q42j-x8rq-pjg6 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-47430
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerability_Management.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Newly patched device that hasn't re-reported to TVM yet still listed as vulnerable (lag of up to 24h)
  • In-house Cordova app rebuilt against 6.0.1 but TVM still recognising the older bundle ID until next scan
  • Third-party MDM-distributed apps where the version string is unparseable and matches the regex spuriously
  • Test/dev iOS devices in an MDM tenant that intentionally hold older app versions for regression testing
  • TVM mis-attributing the npm package version to a wrapping app's own version string
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareName has "cordova-plugin-inappbrowser" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "6.0.1" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "6.1" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "7."
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull DeviceName + LoggedOnUsers for each hit. Confirm the host actually runs an app shipping cordova-plugin-inappbrowser via MDM/Intune app inventory (TVM occasionally flags packages bundled in dead code). Cross-reference with the corporate app catalogue to identify whether the affected app is internally developed or third-party. Step 2 — Contain: For internally-developed apps, open a ticket with the mobile dev team to bump the dependency to ≥6.0.1 and ship a forced-update release; for third-party apps, check the vendor's advisory channel for a patched build and use Intune/Jamf to force-upgrade or block the older version via app protection policy. Step 3 — Hunt: For any device that opens InAppBrowser to OAuth or deep-link redirect targets, review recent UrlClickEvents / SigninLogs for the affected users in the last 30 days for forged-callback indicators (anomalous OAuth consent grants, unexpected account.upn changes on the user's mailbox/contact lists).
// Hunt managed iOS/mobile devices reporting CVE-2026-47430 in TVM
let TargetCve = "CVE-2026-47430";
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId =~ TargetCve
   or (SoftwareName has "cordova-plugin-inappbrowser" and SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^(3\.[1-9]|[3-5]\.\d+|6\.0\.0)")
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, OSVersion, DeviceType, IsInternetFacing, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId
  ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, DeviceType,
          SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel,
          RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, LoggedOnUsers
| extend AffectedRange = "3.1.0 - 6.0.0", FixedVersion = "6.0.1"
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
// Sentinel: same TVM-backed hunt for CVE-2026-47430 on managed mobile assets
let TargetCve = "CVE-2026-47430";
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId =~ TargetCve
   or (SoftwareName has "cordova-plugin-inappbrowser" and SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^(3\.[1-9]|[3-5]\.\d+|6\.0\.0)")
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, OSPlatform, OSVersion, DeviceType, IsInternetFacing, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId
  ) on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, DeviceType,
          SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel,
          RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, LoggedOnUsers
| extend AffectedRange = "3.1.0 - 6.0.0", FixedVersion = "6.0.1"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-47430")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-47430")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VerdantBamboo Deploys BSD Variant of BRICKSTORM on Linux Appliances

The Hacker News
2026-06-08 14 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A China-nexus cyber espionage group has been observed deploying a BSD variant of a known backdoor called BRICKSTORM, as well as two other malware families codenamed PLENET (aka GRIMBOLT) and AGENTPSD to target Linux systems. The activity has been attributed by Volexity to a threat cluster it tracks as VerdantBamboo, which it said overlaps with hacking groups known as Clay Typhoon (Microsoft),

M365 / Entra sign-ins sourced from BRICKSTORM C2 IP 149.248.11.71 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts Microsoft 365 / Entra ID sign-in events whose source IP matches the VerdantBamboo C2 address published by Volexity. Because the actor proxied through compromised Egnyte Storage Sync + pfSense BRICKSTORM SOCKS relays to blend into Conditional Access policies, any direct sign-in from this IP indicates either a misconfigured tunnel or direct actor probing. Rationale: 149.248.11.71 is the sole IP IOC published by Volexity and reposted by Bleeping Computer / Cybersecuritynews — high-fidelity point IOC. Cross-checked Volexity report and Mallory.ai write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-apt-deploys-new-malware-to-keep-access-to-hacked-networks/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019e9476-afd4-71fe-a6f0-7dff94b7f250
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1090.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel team manually validating the IOC via a proxy from this IP
  • Penetration-test engagement deliberately replaying the IOC
  • Shared NAT environment where the same hosting provider IP is used by a legitimate SaaS the org consumes
  • An incident-response vendor using infrastructure in the same /24 subnet
Suppression filter
| where ClientAppUsed !in ("Browser")
| where UserAgent !has "Mozilla"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull every SigninLogs row from 149.248.11.71 in the last 30d, capture UPN, AppDisplayName, ConditionalAccessStatus, and SessionId. Cross-reference UserAgent / ClientAppUsed for non-browser tokens (Exchange ActiveSync, IMAP, REST). 2) CONTAIN: revoke refresh tokens for every UPN seen (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken), force MFA re-enrolment, and add 149.248.11.71 to a Conditional Access named-location block. 3) HUNT: pivot on each affected UPN — search EmailEvents / OfficeActivity for the prior 18 months for mailbox-rule creation, MailItemsAccessed bursts, and OAuth app-consent grants; review SSL VPN logs for sessions matching the same UPN to surface the lateral path from Storage Sync to M365.
AADSignInEventsBeta

| where IPAddress == "149.248.11.71"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Application, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, ErrorCode, Country
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress == "149.248.11.71"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, ResultType, Location
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VerdantBamboo BRICKSTORM / PLENET / AGENTPSD file-hash IOCs AIInstallation Medium
Point-detection on the eight SHA256, four SHA1 and four MD5 hashes Volexity published for the BSD BRICKSTORM variant, PLENET (.NET AOT) and AGENTPSD (Python reverse shell). Matches across DeviceFileEvents and DeviceProcessEvents so we catch both landing and execution attempts on any Defender-for-Linux / Windows host. Rationale: All 16 hashes published in Volexity's June 2026 Verdant Bamboo blog; cross-checked against the BleepingComputer reposting of the IOC list. Hash detections have negligible FP rate; the broader IOC pivot covers the three malware families (BRICKSTORM BSD, PLENET, AGENTPSD) listed in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-apt-deploys-new-malware-to-keep-access-to-hacked-networks/ • https://github.com/mandiant/brickstorm-scanner
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1505.003 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR / forensic analyst detonating a copy of the sample in a sandbox VM connected to the EDR backbone
  • Threat-intel feed reingest dropping the hash into a TI lookup file the EDR then scans
  • AV product quarantine writing the sample to a vendor-managed quarantine folder
  • Reverse-engineer workstation hosting a deliberately retained copy of the binary
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Quarantine"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull every event for the matching hash and identify the binary's drop path, parent process and signer status. For PLENET / BRICKSTORM samples on Linux/BSD appliances, run Mandiant's brickstorm-scanner Bash script against the filesystem to confirm. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host via MDE Machine Isolation (or the appliance equivalent — block at firewall, kill SSH session). Reset credentials cached on the device, especially any service / admin accounts pinned to the Storage Sync / pfSense / NAS appliance. 3) HUNT: pivot every hash hit on its DeviceId across the prior 18 months (the actor's reported dwell time) for AsepValueUpdate / DeviceRegistryEvents persistence, lateral SSH/SMB sessions out of the host, and any M365 OAuth grants under accounts that logged into the host.

AGENTPSD-style Python reverse shell spawned by sshd on Linux / NAS AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the AGENTPSD deployment pattern Volexity describes: VerdantBamboo SSHed into Synology NAS / Linux appliances and dropped a Python-based reverse shell. Surfaces python3 / python processes whose parent is sshd and which subsequently open an outbound socket — a behaviour pattern that survives even when the static hashes mutate. Rationale: The article specifically calls out AGENTPSD as a Python reverse shell deployed over SSH to the Synology NAS. Parent=sshd + child=python is a tight behavioural pair on appliances where Python is rarely launched interactively; the cmd-line tokens are the canonical Python reverse-shell idioms. Cross-checked Volexity blog for the deployment vector (SSH). Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/chinese-apt-verdantbamboo-uses-brickstorm-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1021.004 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible / SaltStack agentless management running ad-hoc python modules over SSH against Linux fleet
  • DevOps engineer using ssh user@host 'python3 -c ...' for debugging
  • Backup / monitoring agent (e.g. Nagios NRPE-compatible Python plugins) invoked through ssh
  • Synology Active Backup / replication daemon when it spawns python from an sshd context
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in ("ansible","saltstack","nagios","nrpe","backup")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: capture the full ProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername and SrcIpAddr of the originating SSH session; correlate against /var/log/auth.log or DeviceLogonEvents to identify the source IP and account that authenticated. 2) CONTAIN: terminate the python PID, kill the parent sshd session, rotate the credential used (especially shared admin / root accounts on the NAS / pfSense / Storage Sync), and add a deny-from rule for the source IP on the appliance's sshd_config or upstream firewall. 3) HUNT: enumerate sibling files dropped under /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, and ~/.cache by the same SSH session; pivot the source IP across NetworkConnectIP4 / VPC flow / firewall logs to see what else it touched; check /etc/cron*, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and systemd unit files for AGENTPSD persistence anchors.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName == "sshd"
| where FileName in~ ("python","python2","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("socket.", "subprocess.", "pty.spawn", "os.dup2", "-c import", "connect((", "/bin/sh", "/bin/bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "sshd"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/python(2|3)?$"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("socket.", "subprocess.", "pty.spawn", "os.dup2", "-c import", "connect((", "/bin/sh", "/bin/bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
title: AGENTPSD-style Python Reverse Shell Spawned by sshd
id: a4127bc8-c5b6-4e5e-b1ec-3f7d4f7c4d31
description: Detects a python interpreter spawned directly by sshd on a Linux / BSD host with command-line arguments matching reverse-shell semantics (socket import, pty.spawn, os.dup2, connect to /bin/sh). Maps to the VerdantBamboo AGENTPSD deployment pattern Volexity documented (June 2026).
references:

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.name:sshd @process.name:(python OR python2 OR python3) @process.command_line:(*socket.* OR *pty.spawn* OR *os.dup2* OR *subprocess.* OR *"/bin/sh"* OR *"/bin/bash"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 #event_platform=Lin
| ParentBaseFileName=/^sshd$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/python(2|3)?$/i
| regex("(socket\.|pty\.spawn|os\.dup2|subprocess\.|-c import|\/bin\/sh|\/bin\/bash)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Outbound endpoint connections to BRICKSTORM C2 IP 149.248.11.71 AICommand & Control Medium
Catches any endpoint, server or appliance making an outbound network connection to the VerdantBamboo BRICKSTORM C2 address. Distinct pivot from UC1 (M365 sign-ins) — this targets the BRICKSTORM SOCKS callback channel rather than the resulting Entra session, so it fires even if the proxy never reaches a successful sign-in. Rationale: 149.248.11.71 is the only network-layer IOC Volexity published. The detection covers every host that BRICKSTORM might call out from (Storage Sync, pfSense, Synology NAS, Windows endpoints) by hitting both EDR and firewall telemetry. Cross-checked Volexity, BleepingComputer and Mallory.ai. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-apt-deploys-new-malware-to-keep-access-to-hacked-networks/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform performing connectivity / sinkhole verification against the published IOC
  • Internal IR sandbox detonating one of the BRICKSTORM samples and reaching the live C2
  • Security researcher / red team simulating the campaign
  • Misconfigured WHOIS / RDAP / passive-DNS enrichment tool that occasionally fetches the IP directly
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","opencti.exe","thehive.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName + DeviceName tuple. If the source is a Linux/BSD appliance (Storage Sync, pfSense, Synology), run Mandiant's brickstorm-scanner against the device's filesystem before touching anything. 2) CONTAIN: sinkhole 149.248.11.71 at the perimeter firewall (drop, not reset), isolate the originating host, and block the IP/24 at the cloud-egress proxy. 3) HUNT: pivot back ≥18 months (the campaign's documented dwell time) on the same DeviceName for ProcessRollup2 of the BRICKSTORM hashes, AsepValueUpdate persistence, SSH lateral movement to NAS hosts, and any sign-in events from internal SSL VPN-range IPs that correspond temporally to BRICKSTORM heartbeats.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "149.248.11.71"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr == "149.248.11.71"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction, SrcUsername),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP == "149.248.11.71"
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, SourceUserName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

pfSense / firewall config change enabling Web SSL VPN after admin login AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the VerdantBamboo re-entry tactic Volexity documents — after stolen admin credentials let them into the firewall, the actor enabled web SSL VPN access to the appliance and used it for ongoing entry. Surfaces config-write events on the firewall WebGUI / SSL VPN service originating from previously-unseen admin source IPs, correlated to a successful admin login in the preceding 15 minutes. Rationale: Volexity explicitly describes the actor reconnecting to the firewall with stolen admin credentials and then enabling web SSL VPN access on the device — Syslog/php-fpm/configd messages on pfSense are the canonical witness for that change. Defender / Falcon are left empty because pfSense appliances are not typically EDR-instrumented; Sigma is left empty because the correlation requires a time-window join between two log events (rule explicitly forbidden for single-event-shape Sigma). Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://cyberpress.org/verdantbamboo-breaches-pfsense-firewall/
ATT&CKT1556 T1133 T1078
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate network admin enabling OpenVPN during a maintenance window
  • Vendor MSP performing planned firmware upgrade and re-enabling services
  • Disaster-recovery failover toggling SSL VPN to the secondary HA pair
  • pfBlocker / pfSense plugin update writing to system_advanced_admin during package install
Suppression filter
| where AdminIP !in ("10.10.10.10","192.168.99.5")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the AdminIP from the joined Syslog row and check whether it is a known internal admin jumpbox / NOC IP; review the diff in pfSense config.xml backups (/cf/conf/backup) around ConfigChangeTime. 2) CONTAIN: roll the firewall config back to the previous known-good backup, disable any newly-added OpenVPN server / user/cert, rotate every local pfSense account (especially `admin`), and revoke any newly-issued OpenVPN certificates. 3) HUNT: cross-reference AdminIP against M365 SigninLogs and SSL VPN session logs for the same window; run Mandiant's brickstorm-scanner against the pfSense filesystem; check /var/etc/openvpn/server*/ for unauthorised client certificates and /etc/inc/services.inc for tampered service hooks.
let AdminLogins = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where Facility in ("auth","authpriv") or ProcessName in ("sshd","webConfigurator","php-fpm")
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("Successful login for user 'admin'", "Successful webConfigurator login", "Accepted password for admin")
    | extend AdminIP = extract(@"from ([\d\.]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | project AdminLoginTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, AdminIP;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ProcessName in ("php-fpm","configd","check_reload_status","openvpn")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("openvpn-server", "server1.conf", "webgui:", "system_advanced_admin", "WebGUI enabled", "User-Manager: 'admin'")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("add","enable","modify","saved")
| join kind=inner AdminLogins on Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (AdminLoginTime .. AdminLoginTime + 15m)
| project AdminLoginTime, ConfigChangeTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, AdminIP, SyslogMessage
| order by ConfigChangeTime desc
source:linux.syslog @host.name:*pfsense* @process.name:(php-fpm OR configd OR check_reload_status OR openvpn) ("openvpn-server" OR "server1.conf" OR "WebGUI enabled" OR "system_advanced_admin" OR "User-Manager: 'admin'")

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Changes.command) as command values(All_Changes.user) as user values(All_Changes.src) as src values(All_Changes.object) as object from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where (All_Changes.object IN ("webconfigurator","openvpn","ssl-vpn","system_advanced_admin") OR All_Changes.command IN ("openvpn-server","webgui-enable","hasync")) (sourcetype="pfsense:filterlog" OR sourcetype="pfsense:configd" OR sourcetype="pfsense") by All_Changes.dest All_Changes.action All_Changes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

UNC3753 Used Vishing and Physical Intrusions in U.S. Data Theft Extortion Campaign

The Hacker News
2026-06-08 18 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a financially motivated data theft extortion campaign that has targeted dozens of organizations across professional, legal, and financial services in the U.S. between January and May 2026. The activity has been attributed by Google Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) to a threat actor dubbed UNC3753, which is also known as

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Quick Assist launched followed by remote interactive session (UNC3753 vishing pretext) · [LLM] Privnote[.]com self-destructing-note URL access from corporate endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AnyDesk, Bomgar, SuperOps or Zoho Assist installer execution (UNC3753 RMM foothold) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to UNC3753 (Luna Moth) infrastructure IPs · [LLM] Outbound mail to or domain lookup of business-data-leaks[.]com (UNC3753 extortion infrastructure) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] WinSCP or Rclone exfiltration from end-user workstations · [LLM] USB mass-storage attached followed by bulk file copy (UNC3753 physical intrusion) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Quick Assist launched followed by remote interactive session (UNC3753 vishing pretext) AIDelivery Medium
Detects users launching Microsoft Quick Assist (quickassist.exe) and then a remote-controlled session beginning shortly after — the UNC3753 pretext for IT-help-desk vishing. Article-specific because UNC3753 explicitly named Quick Assist alongside Zoom/Teams as the screen-share entry vector. Rationale: Article names Quick Assist explicitly as a vector. The binary is fairly rare in most enterprises (Teams/Zoom are more common), so plain execution is a hunt-grade pivot. Corroborated with CISA & Microsoft advisories on Storm-1811/Quick Assist abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/05/15/threat-actors-misusing-quick-assist-in-social-engineering-attacks-leading-to-ransomware/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
ATT&CKT1219 T1566.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate corporate IT desktop support sessions
  • End-user-initiated Microsoft support call (consumer)
  • Quick Assist used as documented MSP onboarding workflow
  • Auto-launched by RemoteAssistance Group Policy on managed laptops
  • Pre-shipped to certain OEM image builds
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("it-helpdesk","corp-support")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user had a recorded ticket with internal IT help desk in the 15 minutes prior. Pull AccountName, DeviceName, and ProcessCommandLine. Pivot to user's mailbox (EmailEvents) for invoice-themed pretexts in last 24h. 2) Contain: if no legitimate ticket, isolate the device via Defender (Isolate Machine), force-reset the user's credentials, revoke active sessions. Block quickassist.exe via AppLocker or WDAC on the user group if Quick Assist is not in your sanctioned remote-support stack. 3) Hunt: pivot on AccountName across DeviceProcessEvents for AnyDesk/Bomgar/SuperOps/Zoho installers in the same 24-hour window, and on DeviceNetworkEvents for the article's UNC3753 IP set.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "quickassist.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "quickassist.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\quickassist.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\quickassist.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Microsoft Quick Assist Execution (UNC3753 Vishing Pretext)
id: 6f2a8b3c-1c7d-4f50-a47b-2a3df9b1a401
description: Detects launch of Microsoft Quick Assist (quickassist.exe), abused by UNC3753/Luna Moth/SRG to obtain remote-control screen-share sessions after vishing IT-helpdesk pretexts.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/unc3753-used-vishing-and-physical.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/08
tags:
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.t1566.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\quickassist.exe'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\quickassist.exe OR *\QuickAssist.exe OR *\QUICKASSIST.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\quickassist\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="quickassist.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="quickassist.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="quickassist.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="quickassist.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
AnyDesk, Bomgar, SuperOps or Zoho Assist installer execution (UNC3753 RMM foothold) AIInstallation Medium
Detects fresh installation or first-time execution of the specific RMM tools UNC3753 instructs vishing victims to install (AnyDesk, Bomgar, SuperOps RMM, Zoho Assist). High-value hunting pivot since the article names these four explicitly. Rationale: Article explicitly names these four RMM tools as the post-vishing foothold mechanism. None should be ubiquitous in an org with a single sanctioned RMM — flag the deviations. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-156a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1020/
ATT&CKT1219 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned MSP using one of the four named tools
  • Sales engineer demo of Zoho or SuperOps
  • End user installs AnyDesk personal edition for home support
  • IT testing alternative RMM during procurement evaluation
  • Vendor support session pre-arranged via ticket
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\Program Files\\<SanctionedRMMVendor>\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: cross-check against your sanctioned RMM allowlist. Pull AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, parent process. Check the user's mail for invoice-themed pretexts and call records / Teams call logs in the prior 60 minutes. 2) Contain: kill the RMM process tree, uninstall, force credential reset, revoke MFA tokens, block the RMM domains at the proxy if unsanctioned. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound to any of the article IPs (192.236.147.131, 192.236.147.138, 193.141.60.212, 192.236.154.158, 192.236.146.173, 174.169.162.62, 64.94.84.97), WinSCP/Rclone usage, and access to highly sensitive folder paths ("tax", "audit", "SSN", "client").
let RMMBinaries = dynamic(["anydesk.exe","bomgar-scc.exe","bomgarportal.exe","bomgar.exe","superops.rmm.agent.exe","superops_agent.exe","zohoassist.exe","zohomeeting.exe","za_connect.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ (RMMBinaries)
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AnyDesk","Bomgar","SuperOps","Zoho Assist")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let RMMBinaries = dynamic(["anydesk.exe","bomgar-scc.exe","bomgarportal.exe","bomgar.exe","superops.rmm.agent.exe","superops_agent.exe","zohoassist.exe","zohomeeting.exe","za_connect.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ProcessFile = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName,"\\")[-1]))
| where ProcessFile in (RMMBinaries)
   or CommandLine has_any ("AnyDesk","Bomgar","SuperOps","Zoho Assist")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: UNC3753 Named RMM Tool Execution (AnyDesk/Bomgar/SuperOps/Zoho Assist)
id: 7d4f9a18-2b6c-4a01-9e3f-b2c5d8e1a002
description: Detects execution of the RMM tools UNC3753 / Luna Moth / Silent Ransom Group instruct victims to install during vishing-driven intrusions.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","BomgarPortal.exe","bomgar-scc.exe","SuperOps.RMM.Agent.exe","ZohoMeeting.exe","ZA_Connect.exe") OR Processes.process IN ("*AnyDesk*","*Bomgar*","*SuperOps*","*ZohoAssist*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
Privnote[.]com self-destructing-note URL access from corporate endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Detects users browsing to privnote.com — the legitimate self-destruct-note service UNC3753 uses to deliver RMM install instructions during vishing calls without leaving recoverable evidence. Article-specific: privnote was explicitly named as the delivery channel. Rationale: Privnote is a legitimate but rarely-business-justified service. Article calls it out as UNC3753's instruction-delivery mechanism — DNS / proxy visibility on it is a cheap, high-signal pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://krebsonsecurity.com/2023/05/phishing-domains-tanked-after-meta-sued-freenom/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/
ATT&CKT1102 T1566.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Journalist / lawyer using privnote for legitimate confidential comms
  • User receives a privnote link from a known counterparty
  • Security researcher pivoting on threat-intel report
  • Personal use during break — non-work browsing
  • HR forwarding a sensitive doc one-time
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user, time of access, and any process that subsequently spawned (RMM installer? PowerShell? cmd?) within 30 minutes. Ask the user directly — privnote use is uncommon. 2) Contain: if user reports an unsolicited helpdesk call, isolate device, reset creds, revoke sessions. 3) Hunt: 7-day org-wide privnote.com lookups to find peer victims; pivot any matching host on RMM execution and outbound to the UNC3753 IP set.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "privnote.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has "privnote.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Privnote Self-Destructing-Note Service Access (UNC3753 Delivery Channel)
id: 8e1a4d72-3b50-4c98-bc12-f9d8a4b25c03
description: Detects access to privnote.com, used by UNC3753 / Luna Moth / SRG to deliver RMM installation instructions to vishing victims.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/08
tags:

  - attack.t1566.004
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|contains: 'privnote.com'
  condition: selection
level: low
@dns.question.name:*privnote.com* OR @http.url:*privnote.com* OR @url:*privnote.com*
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/privnote\.com$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*privnote.com*" OR Web.dest="privnote.com" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*privnote.com*" OR Web.dest="privnote.com" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
Outbound connection to UNC3753 (Luna Moth) infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any endpoint or network egress to the seven IPs Mandiant/GTIG tied to UNC3753 (192.236.147.131, 192.236.147.138, 193.141.60.212, 192.236.154.158, 192.236.146.173, 174.169.162.62, 64.94.84.97). High-confidence alerting tier since these are specific IOCs. Rationale: Seven specific IOCs from the article — second-source corroborated against Mandiant/GTIG attribution to UNC3753 and FBI advisory. Direct-IP detections are high fidelity and low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1020/ • https://www.ic3.gov/Media/News/2024/240712.pdf
ATT&CKT1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Network
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher sandbox testing IOCs
  • Honeypot or red-team simulating UNC3753
  • Penetration test engagement using same IP range
  • Legitimate co-tenant on shared hosting provider (192.236.0.0/16 is ColoCrossing)
  • Crowd-sourced threat feed false-positive ingest
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandbox.exe","cuckoo.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host, user, and process making the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName). Determine session length and byte counts — short HTTPS probes vs sustained file uploads tell very different stories. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender, block the IP at perimeter (firewall + EDR network containment), reset user creds & revoke MFA. 3) Hunt: 30-day lookback across the org on the same IP set; pivot on any host that hit it for WinSCP/Rclone exfil, Quick Assist/AnyDesk/Bomgar/SuperOps/Zoho Assist execution, and access to sensitive folder paths.
let UNC3753_IPs = dynamic(["192.236.147.131","192.236.147.138","193.141.60.212","192.236.154.158","192.236.146.173","174.169.162.62","64.94.84.97"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (UNC3753_IPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let UNC3753_IPs = dynamic(["192.236.147.131","192.236.147.138","193.141.60.212","192.236.154.158","192.236.146.173","174.169.162.62","64.94.84.97"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (UNC3753_IPs)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, EventVendor, EventProduct, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WinSCP or Rclone exfiltration from end-user workstations AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects WinSCP and Rclone process execution from user-context endpoints — UNC3753's named exfiltration tooling for staged sensitive data. Filters out IT-admin and backup-team baseline use. Rationale: Article names WinSCP and Rclone as the staged-exfil tooling. Both binaries are extremely rare in finance/legal services user contexts. Strong hunt-grade signal when scoped away from backup/IT. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1040/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-061a
ATT&CKT1567 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps engineer pushing files to staging SFTP
  • Backup admin orchestrating cloud snapshots
  • Security team red-team data-exfil simulation
  • Database admin transferring schemas between regions
  • Developer using rclone with personal Google Drive remote
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("backupsvc","sftpsvc","devops") or DeviceName has_any ("backup","jumpbox","bastion","ci-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the executing user has any documented business reason for WinSCP/Rclone (DevOps role? backup duties?). Pull full CommandLine — look for SFTP/FTPS/S3/GDrive remotes and the source path ("Documents", "Client", "Tax", "Audit"). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, block outbound on suspected destination, reset user creds and revoke sessions. Preserve volumes for forensics — extortion follow-up email may land within 30 minutes. 3) Hunt: pivot user/host for prior Quick Assist/AnyDesk/Bomgar/SuperOps/Zoho Assist execution, sensitive-folder enumeration (large numbers of file reads under client/tax/audit paths), and outbound to UNC3753 IP set.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("winscp.exe","winscp.com","rclone.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rclone copy","rclone sync","rclone copyto","winscp.com /command","open sftp://","open ftps://")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("backupsvc","sftpsvc"))
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("backup","jumpbox","bastion"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ProcessFile = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName,"\\")[-1]))
| where ProcessFile in ("winscp.exe","winscp.com","rclone.exe")
   or CommandLine has_any ("rclone copy","rclone sync","rclone copyto","winscp.com /command","open sftp://","open ftps://")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where not (SubjectUserName has_any ("backupsvc","sftpsvc"))
| where not (Computer has_any ("backup","jumpbox","bastion"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

USB mass-storage attached followed by bulk file copy (UNC3753 physical intrusion) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects USB mass-storage attach events followed within 30 minutes by a high volume of file writes/reads against the device — modelling the FBI-reported UNC3753 escalation where threat actors enter offices in person posing as IT technicians and exfiltrate via external USB drives. Rationale: FBI advisory and the article both call out the new in-person USB-exfil escalation. Removable-media + bulk-write correlation on the user's workstation is the only telemetry surface for this physical-intrusion variant. Image [1] (vishing.jpg) reinforces the broader social-engineering pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/Media/News/2024/240712.pdf • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1052/001/
ATT&CKT1052.001 T1200
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee transferring large dataset to encrypted corporate USB
  • Executive copying presentation deck to USB before travel
  • Field engineer offloading sensor data from removable disk
  • Marketing team archiving event photos to portable SSD
  • IT asset transfer / device retirement workflow
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("backupsvc","itsupport")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user account was physically on-site at attach time (badge logs, camera). Pull the AdditionalFields blob for USB vendor/serial. Check the user's tickets/calendar for an authorised IT visit. 2) Contain: revoke active sessions, suspend the account pending interview, isolate the host, and disable USB mass-storage class via GPO for the affected device. Preserve the workstation image. 3) Hunt: pivot the USB vendor/serial across the org — same drive on multiple hosts indicates a roaming insider/attacker. Cross-check physical access logs for unfamiliar visitors and review camera footage covering the attach time window.
let USBAttach = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("UsbDriveMounted","PnpDeviceConnected","UsbDriveDriveLetterChanged")
    | project AttachTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, AdditionalFields;
let BulkCopy = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | where FolderPath matches regex @"^[D-Z]:\\"
    | summarize FileCount = count(), FirstWrite=min(Timestamp), LastWrite=max(Timestamp), SampleFile=any(FolderPath) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
    | where FileCount > 50;
USBAttach
| join kind=inner BulkCopy on DeviceId
| where FirstWrite between (AttachTime .. AttachTime + 30m)
| project AttachTime, FirstWrite, LastWrite, DeviceName, AccountName, FileCount, SampleFile, AdditionalFields
| order by AttachTime desc
let USBAttach = Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventLog == "Microsoft-Windows-DriverFrameworks-UserMode/Operational"
       or (EventLog == "System" and EventID in (20001,20003))
    | project AttachTime=TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID;
let BulkCopy = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4663
    | where ObjectName matches regex @"^[D-Z]:\\"
    | summarize FileCount = count(), FirstAccess=min(TimeGenerated), LastAccess=max(TimeGenerated), SampleFile=any(ObjectName) by Computer, AccountName=SubjectUserName
    | where FileCount > 50;
USBAttach
| join kind=inner BulkCopy on Computer
| where FirstAccess between (AttachTime .. AttachTime + 30m)
| project AttachTime, FirstAccess, LastAccess, Computer, AccountName, FileCount, SampleFile
| order by AttachTime desc
source:windows.security @EventID:6416 @ClassName:DiskDrive
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/^[D-Z]:\\\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count(as=FileCount))
| FileCount > 50
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" AND Filesystem.file_path IN ("E:\\*","F:\\*","G:\\*","H:\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count > 50 AND firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" AND Filesystem.file_path IN ("E:\\*","F:\\*","G:\\*","H:\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count > 50 AND firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
Outbound mail to or domain lookup of business-data-leaks[.]com (UNC3753 extortion infrastructure) AICommand & Control High
Detects communications with business-data-leaks.com — the UNC3753 / Luna Moth data-leak-site domain referenced in extortion follow-ups. Any DNS lookup or email contact with this domain from the enterprise indicates either an in-progress extortion or a curious researcher. Rationale: Domain explicitly referenced in the article (LEAKEDDATA leak site) and corroborated by Mandiant attribution. Hits should be near-zero in normal enterprise traffic. Image [2] (LEAKEDDATA.png) corroborates the leak-site branding. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1020/ • https://www.ic3.gov/Media/News/2024/240712.pdf
ATT&CKT1567 T1657
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Email.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst pivoting on indicators
  • Legal team reviewing leak-site exposure of own client data
  • Sandbox detonation of a sample referencing the domain
  • CTI feed pre-fetching domain metadata
  • DLP scanner accessing dark/clear-web monitoring tool
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify whether the source is an end-user host (likely breach) or threat-intel pivot host (expected). Pull DNS / web logs and any inbound email from the domain. Search mailbox for extortion-style language ("three-day deadline", "data breach", "published"). 2) Contain: if end-user origin — declare incident, engage IR/legal/privacy, force credential reset across exposed user accounts, isolate originating host, preserve mailbox. 3) Hunt: 90-day org-wide lookup for the domain; pivot to UNC3753 IPs, WinSCP/Rclone runs, AnyDesk/Bomgar/SuperOps/Zoho Assist installations, and Quick Assist sessions to scope the incident.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has "business-data-leaks.com" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="DeviceNetworkEvents", InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP),
(EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SenderFromAddress has "business-data-leaks.com" or SenderMailFromDomain has "business-data-leaks.com" | project Timestamp, DeviceName="", Source="EmailEvents", InitiatingProcessAccountName=RecipientEmailAddress, InitiatingProcessFileName=Subject, RemoteUrl=SenderFromAddress, RemoteIP="")
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has "business-data-leaks.com" | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Indicator=DnsQuery),
(OfficeActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Operation has_any ("Send","MailItemsAccessed") | where tostring(EventData) has "business-data-leaks.com" | project TimeGenerated, Source="Office365", SrcHostname="", SrcIpAddr=ClientIP, SrcUsername=UserId, Indicator="business-data-leaks.com")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
