Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.

DeviceProcessEvents

        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

AuditLogs

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"

status: experimental

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-42271", "CVE-2026-48710")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-42271", "CVE-2026-48710")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

SecurityEvent

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Free Apps Are Quietly Turning Smart TVs Into Web-Scraping Proxies for AI

The Hacker News
2026-06-06 9 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A researcher has reverse-engineered the iOS SDK that Bright Data embeds in consumer apps and documented how it turns devices, including always-on smart TVs, into exit nodes that relay web-scraping traffic for a data business Bright Data markets heavily to the AI industry. The company, the successor to Luminati, operates what it calls the largest residential proxy network in the world,

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Bright Data partner-app or brdsdk.framework present on managed iOS / mobile inventory
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Bright Data SDK control-plane beacon to proxyjs/clientsdk endpoints · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Bright Data SDK control-plane beacon to proxyjs/clientsdk endpoints AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS or TLS SNI resolution to the Bright Data residential-proxy SDK control channels (proxyjs/clientsdk on bright-sdk.com, brdtnet.com, luminatinet.com). Any endpoint resolving these is either running an app embedding brdsdk.framework or actively relaying scraping jobs as an exit node. Rationale: All five FQDNs (proxyjs.brdtnet.com, proxyjs.luminatinet.com, proxyjs.bright-sdk.com, clientsdk.bright-sdk.com, clientsdk.brdtnet.com) are explicitly named in the article body and corroborated by the Include Security research blog as the SDK's exclusive control-plane channel — the article itself recommends blocking them at the router. The article also notes Bright Data's paid commercial service runs on different hosts, so hits here are specifically the embedded-SDK exit-node behaviour. Cross-checked against the Include Security research blog (https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/) which added the broader *.luminati.io SNI pattern and the brdsdk.framework binary identifier. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data-engineering team running a sanctioned Bright Data paid scraper proof-of-concept and pointing it at the shared SDN endpoints
  • Security researcher VM (e.g. malware sandbox, threat-intel analyst) intentionally executing a partner app to reproduce the Include Security teardown
  • DNS resolver / threat-intel feed cache pre-resolving newly-published IOCs without an actual user-driven query
  • Corporate guest WiFi hosting employee BYOD smart-TV streaming sticks or phones that have a Bright Data partner app installed
  • Vendor or supplier remote-access laptops where users installed Petflix-style free consumer apps off-hours
Suppression filter
// Suppress sanctioned Bright Data paid-service test hosts (uncomment and populate)
// | where DeviceName !in~ ("scraping-poc-01","data-eng-vm-bd")
// Suppress sandbox/researcher subnets
// | where ipv4_is_in_any_range(RemoteIP, dynamic(["10.99.0.0/24"])) == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the resolving asset from Defender DeviceInfo / DHCP — is it a corp endpoint, a managed iPhone, a smart TV on guest VLAN, or unknown IoT? Confirm InitiatingProcessFileName on Defender hits (iOS will surface the host app bundle ID; corp Windows hitting these is unusual and a separate concern). 2) Contain: Sinkhole all five FQDNs and the *.bright-sdk.com / *.brdtnet.com / *.luminatinet.com / *.luminati.io suffixes at the corporate DNS resolver and egress firewall; if the asset is a corp-issued iPhone, push an Intune compliance check that blocks the offending host app. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the source IP across the last 30 days of NetFlow / proxy logs for sustained high-fan-out HTTPS egress (UC3 logic); query DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory and Intune app inventory for any other devices reporting the same partner-app bundle so you can scope the affected fleet.
// Bright Data residential-proxy SDK control-plane beacon
// Endpoints contacting *.bright-sdk.com / *.brdtnet.com / *.luminatinet.com
let brdControlHosts = dynamic(["proxyjs.brdtnet.com","proxyjs.luminatinet.com","proxyjs.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.brdtnet.com"]);
let brdSuffixes = dynamic([".bright-sdk.com",".brdtnet.com",".luminatinet.com",".luminati.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (brdControlHosts)
    or RemoteUrl has_any (brdSuffixes)
| extend MatchType = case(RemoteUrl in~ (brdControlHosts), "control-plane FQDN",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".bright-sdk.com", "bright-sdk.com suffix",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".brdtnet.com", "brdtnet.com suffix",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".luminatinet.com", "luminatinet.com suffix",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".luminati.io", "luminati.io suffix",
                          "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, MatchType
| order by Timestamp desc
// Bright Data residential-proxy SDK control-plane beacon — ASIM DNS view
let brdControlHosts = dynamic(["proxyjs.brdtnet.com","proxyjs.luminatinet.com","proxyjs.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.brdtnet.com"]);
let brdSuffixes = dynamic([".bright-sdk.com",".brdtnet.com",".luminatinet.com",".luminati.io"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where DnsQuery in~ (brdControlHosts)
       or DnsQuery has_any (brdSuffixes)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Indicator = DnsQuery, Source = "ImDnsActivity"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where isnotempty(DestinationHostName)
   | where DestinationHostName in~ (brdControlHosts)
       or DestinationHostName has_any (brdSuffixes)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, SrcHostname = SourceHostName, SrcUsername = SourceUserName,
             Indicator = DestinationHostName, Source = strcat(DeviceVendor,"/",DeviceProduct)),
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where Name has_any (brdSuffixes) or Name in~ (brdControlHosts)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = ClientIP, SrcHostname = Computer, SrcUsername = "", Indicator = Name, Source = "DnsEvents"))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(),
            Indicators = make_set(Indicator, 25), Sources = make_set(Source, 5)
            by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| order by LastSeen desc

Bright Data partner-app or brdsdk.framework present on managed iOS / mobile inventory AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the managed mobile/endpoint fleet for installed apps that ship the Bright Data residential-proxy SDK (brdsdk.framework v1.532.120) — using the article-named partner-app list (Petflix, PlayWorks Digital, CloudTV, Longvision) and Bright Data's published partner page. Catches the exit-node *at install time* rather than waiting for it to phone home. Rationale: Article explicitly names Petflix (Roku), PlayWorks Digital, CloudTV, and Longvision as Bright Data partners shipping the SDK, and identifies brdsdk.framework v1.532.120 as the binary. Include Security additionally surfaced the Swift symbols BrdWebSocketFacade and BrdNetwork.DNSResolver inside the framework. Article notes the partner list is not 1:1 with current SDK inclusion (each app must be verified independently), so this is a hunt not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1474.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Software
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security research team intentionally side-loaded the partner app on a managed device to reproduce the teardown
  • Employee BYOD device enrolled in MDM with a legitimately-installed free TV/streaming app where the developer has since removed the SDK
  • Partner-app vendor whitelisted by Procurement for a specific business use case (e.g. a marketing team approved CloudTV for an ad campaign monitor)
  • Generic name collision — "PlayWorks" or "CloudTV" could match unrelated apps; verify the bundle ID against Bright Data's published partner page
  • Inventory delay — an app uninstalled hours ago may still show in DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory until the next sync
Suppression filter
// Exclude approved BD test devices (populate with your scraping-POC fleet)
// | where DeviceName !in~ ("sec-research-ios-01","sec-research-ios-02")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the exact bundle ID / package name from DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory and cross-check against Bright Data's public partner page; eliminate name-collision FPs. Confirm whether the device has actually beaconed to the UC1 control-plane domains within 14 days. 2) Contain: Add the confirmed bundle IDs to the Intune / MDM compromised-app list and force-uninstall on managed devices; for BYOD, push a compliance policy that blocks corporate resource access until the app is removed. 3) Hunt: Pivot DeviceImageLoadEvents on any device for the brdsdk.framework load event or the Swift symbols BrdWebSocketFacade / BrdNetwork.DNSResolver to find apps not on the published partner list that nonetheless embed the SDK.
// Hunt managed fleet for Bright Data SDK partner apps and the brdsdk.framework binary
let brdPartnerApps = dynamic(["Petflix","PlayWorks","CloudTV","Longvision"]);
let brdVendors = dynamic(["PlayWorks Digital","CloudTV","Longvision","Bright Data","Luminati"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has_any (brdPartnerApps)
    or SoftwareVendor has_any (brdVendors)
    or SoftwareName contains "brdsdk"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, DeviceType, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, DeviceType, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers, EndOfSupportStatus
| union (
    DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName contains "brdsdk" or FolderPath contains "brdsdk.framework" or FileName has_any ("BrdWebSocketFacade","BrdNetwork")
    | project DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
  )
| order by DeviceName asc
// Hunt managed fleet (Defender via Sentinel + Intune) for Bright Data SDK partner apps
let brdPartnerApps = dynamic(["Petflix","PlayWorks","CloudTV","Longvision"]);
let brdVendors = dynamic(["PlayWorks Digital","CloudTV","Longvision","Bright Data","Luminati"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has_any (brdPartnerApps)
    or SoftwareVendor has_any (brdVendors)
    or SoftwareName contains "brdsdk"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, OSPlatform, DeviceType, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, DeviceType, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, PublicIP

Smart-TV / mobile device acting as residential proxy exit node (high-fan-out HTTPS to unrelated public destinations) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts firewall and NetFlow telemetry for the behavioural signature of a Bright Data exit node: a single internal source (typically an unmanaged smart TV or mobile device) initiates a high volume of outbound HTTPS sessions to many unrelated public web destinations the user is not actively browsing, often during off-hours. The 200 GB/month SDK cap and the device's always-on TV / mobile profile shape the threshold. Rationale: Article quantifies the SDK's monthly traffic ceiling (200 GB/mo, uncapped in some regions) and notes the device 'keeps relaying in the background while someone is watching the screen or on a call, as long as the battery is not low'. The behavioural fingerprint — single internal source, hundreds of unrelated public destinations per hour, outbound bytes ≈ inbound bytes (proxy relay, not browsing) — is what survives even if Bright Data rotates control-plane domains. Article warns 'Bright Data could also change how the SDK connects in the future, which would mean any blocklist needs updating' which is exactly why a behavioural UC complements UC1's IOC UC. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1496 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate VPN concentrator or split-tunnel egress gateway — many destinations, high volume, but the source IP is a known infrastructure host
  • Marketing / SEO crawler or competitive-intelligence scraping VM the business legitimately runs
  • Backup appliance or DR replication target uploading to many regional cloud endpoints
  • Smart-home hub (e.g. Home Assistant, Hubitat) polling dozens of cloud APIs concurrently from an IoT VLAN
  • Update server / mirror replicating from many upstream package repositories during a patch window
Suppression filter
// Exclude known infrastructure egress points (VPN concentrators, web crawlers, backup targets)
// | where SourceIP !in ("10.10.5.20","10.10.5.21","10.20.1.0/24")
// Exclude SEO/marketing crawlers
// | where SourceHostName !startswith "crawl-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Map SourceIP to asset via DHCP, NAC, or DeviceInfo — is it a managed endpoint, a known infrastructure host (VPN/proxy/crawler), or unattributed IoT/guest? Pull a 24h destination-host sample and look for residential-proxy tells: unrelated industries, geographic spread, e-commerce/news/forum mix, no clear business affinity. 2) Contain: If asset is unmanaged smart TV or guest-network device, quarantine VLAN port and apply the UC1 sinkhole; if it's a managed iPhone, push Intune block on the offending host app and confirm via UC2 inventory. 3) Hunt: Cross-correlate SourceIP with UC1 hits in the prior 14 days; check whether the same MAC/asset has historically resolved any *.bright-sdk.com / *.brdtnet.com / *.luminatinet.com; pull NetFlow byte-out trend for the device for the prior 30 days to confirm sustained 200GB/month pacing.
// Managed iOS / mobile exhibiting residential-proxy egress pattern (covers Defender for iOS estate)
let WindowHrs = 1h;
let MinUniqueRemoteIPs = 100;   // residential browsing rarely fans out to >100 distinct public IPs per hour
let MinSessions = 500;          // SDK polling + scraping job throughput floor
let ManagedMobile = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(24h)
    | where OSPlatform in ("iOS","iPadOS","Android")
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, DeviceType, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| join kind=inner ManagedMobile on DeviceId
| summarize UniqueRemoteIPs = dcount(RemoteIP),
            UniqueRemoteUrls = dcount(RemoteUrl),
            Sessions = count(),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 25),
            SampleProcess = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, bin(Timestamp, WindowHrs)
| where UniqueRemoteIPs > MinUniqueRemoteIPs and Sessions > MinSessions
| extend MultiUseSig = iff(UniqueRemoteUrls > 200 and array_length(SampleProcess) <= 2, "likely-proxy", "review")
| order by Sessions desc
// Residential-proxy exit-node behavioural hunt against firewall logs
// Surfaces internal sources fan-out HTTPS to many unrelated public destinations (Bright Data exit-node signature)
let WindowHrs = 1h;
let MinUniqueDests = 250;       // home/IoT devices very rarely exceed this per hour
let MinBytesOut = 524288000;    // 500 MB outbound per hour (200 GB/mo SDK cap → ~280 MB/hr avg, peaks higher)
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceVendor in ("Palo Alto Networks","Fortinet","Cisco","Check Point","Zscaler","SonicWall")
| where DestinationPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and isnotempty(DestinationIP)
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| summarize UniqueDestHosts = dcount(DestinationHostName),
            UniqueDestIPs = dcount(DestinationIP),
            BytesOut = sum(toint(SentBytes)),
            BytesIn = sum(toint(ReceivedBytes)),
            Sessions = count(),
            SampleHosts = make_set(DestinationHostName, 25)
            by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowHrs)
| where UniqueDestHosts > MinUniqueDests and BytesOut > MinBytesOut
| extend GbOut = round(BytesOut / 1073741824.0, 2)
| extend EgressInboundRatio = round(BytesOut * 1.0 / (BytesIn + 1), 2)
| where EgressInboundRatio > 0.4   // proxy traffic: outbound ~= inbound, unlike normal browsing which is inbound-heavy
| order by BytesOut desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true 
    dc(All_Traffic.dest) as uniqueDests 
    dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as uniqueDstIPs 
    sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytesOut 
    sum(All_Traffic.bytes_in) as bytesIn 
    count as connCount 
    values(All_Traffic.app) as apps 
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic 
    where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (80,443) AND All_Traffic.action=allowed 
    by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_category _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")`
| where uniqueDests > 250 AND bytesOut > 524288000
| eval gbOut = round(bytesOut/1073741824, 2)
| where src_category IN ("iot","smart_tv","mobile","unknown","guest")
| sort - bytesOut
| tstats summariesonly=false 
    dc(All_Traffic.dest) as uniqueDests 
    dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as uniqueDstIPs 
    sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytesOut 
    sum(All_Traffic.bytes_in) as bytesIn 
    count as connCount 
    values(All_Traffic.app) as apps 
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic 
    where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (80,443) AND All_Traffic.action=allowed 
    by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_category _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")`
| where uniqueDests > 250 AND bytesOut > 524288000
| eval gbOut = round(bytesOut/1073741824, 2)
| where src_category IN ("iot","smart_tv","mobile","unknown","guest")
| sort - bytesOut
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

GitHub Security Advisories
2026-06-05 2 use cases 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

Shopper: Authorization bypass and RBAC privilege escalation in team settings

CVEsCVE-2026-47744

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] HTTP access to Shopper admin team-settings / Livewire endpoints (CVE-2026-47744)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
HTTP access to Shopper admin team-settings / Livewire endpoints (CVE-2026-47744) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the vulnerable Shopper admin panel routes — Settings/Team/Index and Settings/Team/RolePermission — including their Livewire AJAX endpoints. Pre-patch (Shopper < 2.8.0) these were reachable by any authenticated panel user and were the only network observable for the authorization-bypass / RBAC privilege-escalation chain disclosed in GHSA-c3qp-2ggw-xjg7. Rationale: The article names exactly two Livewire components — Settings/Team/Index and Settings/Team/RolePermission — as the abuse surface. Livewire routes those component names verbatim through /livewire/update (Livewire v3) and /livewire/message/{component} (v2), so the component string and these endpoints are the highest-fidelity strings available pre-exploit. POST/PUT/PATCH on the role-permission route is the specific action that grants/escalates permissions, distinguishing exploitation from normal page loads. No external IOC corroboration was attempted since the advisory exposes no network IOCs — only source-code paths.
ATT&CKT1190 T1068 T1078.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Shopper panel administrators (manage_users holders) creating roles or updating role permissions in normal operations
  • Internal QA / penetration-test exercises against the upgraded (>=2.8.0) panel
  • Application monitoring/uptime probes hitting the admin panel index without authentication (will 302 to login but still appear in HTTP logs)
  • Crawlers / bots probing /livewire/update on any Livewire-built site (broad Livewire scanners)
  • Reverse-proxy retries duplicating the same POST to /livewire/update on transient 5xx
Suppression filter
| where not (User in~ ("admin","superadmin") and ClientIP in ("10.0.0.0/8","192.168.0.0/16")) and not (UserAgent has_any ("Pingdom","UptimeRobot","StatusCake"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the Shopper composer.lock from the affected host and confirm shopper/framework < 2.8.0; if patched, downgrade severity. Identify the authenticated session behind the request (panel session cookie or X-Forwarded-User) and map to the panel user — was it a holder of view_users only? 2) Contain: force-logout all panel sessions, rotate panel admin credentials, and either upgrade to shopper/framework 2.8.0 immediately or block /livewire/update and /admin/settings/team* at the WAF until upgrade. 3) Hunt: dump the roles and role_permission tables and diff against a known-good snapshot — look for newly granted manage_users / edit_orders to non-admin accounts; review the panel users table for unexpected deletions of legitimate administrators; pivot on the source IP across the prior 30 days for any other panel reconnaissance.
// Requires IIS / nginx access logs ingested to a custom table; M365 Defender XDR does not natively capture inbound HTTP to a self-hosted PHP app.
// Pivot via DeviceNetworkEvents for the web server's inbound traffic to the panel's listening port, then triage in the proxy/WAF.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","php-fpm.exe","php.exe","nginx.exe","httpd.exe","caddy.exe")
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where Connections > 5
| order by LastSeen desc
let TargetPaths = dynamic(["settings/team","settings.team.index","settings.team.role-permission","settings.team.rolepermission","/livewire/update","/livewire/message/settings.team"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
    (W3CIISLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where csUriStem has_any (TargetPaths) or csUriQuery has_any (TargetPaths)
        | project TimeGenerated, Source="IIS", Computer, Method=csMethod, Url=strcat(csUriStem, iff(isnotempty(csUriQuery), strcat("?", csUriQuery), "")), Status=scStatus, ClientIP=cIP, UserAgent=csUserAgent, User=csUserName),
    (AppServiceHTTPLogs
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where CsUriStem has_any (TargetPaths) or CsUriQuery has_any (TargetPaths)
        | project TimeGenerated, Source="AppService", Computer=CsHost, Method=CsMethod, Url=strcat(CsUriStem, iff(isnotempty(CsUriQuery), strcat("?", CsUriQuery), "")), Status=ScStatus, ClientIP=CIp, UserAgent=UserAgent, User=CsUsername),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where RequestURL has_any (TargetPaths)
        | project TimeGenerated, Source=DeviceProduct, Computer=DestinationHostName, Method=RequestMethod, Url=RequestURL, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), ClientIP=SourceIP, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, User=SourceUserName)
)
| where Method in~ ("POST","PUT","PATCH") or Url has_any ("role-permission","rolepermission")
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Methods = make_set(Method), Statuses = make_set(Status), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5), Users = make_set(User, 10) by ClientIP, Computer, Source
| order by LastSeen desc

references:

[GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-47731: NASA AMMOS Instrument Toolkit: Path traversal resulting in arbitrary file append (can be triggered over the network by unauthenticated attacker)

GitHub Security Advisories
2026-06-05 4 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

NASA AMMOS Instrument Toolkit: Path traversal resulting in arbitrary file append (can be triggered over the network by unauthenticated attacker)

CVEsCVE-2026-47731
ATT&CKT1190
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
Detected
Phase 2
Weaponization
—
Phase 3
Delivery
—
Phase 4
Exploitation
Detected
Phase 5
Installation
Likely
Phase 6
Command & Control
Detected
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated POST to AIT-BSC /<name>/start with path-traversal form fields (CVE-2026-47731) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-47731: NASA AMMOS Instrument Toolkit: Path traversal
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ait-bsc outbound TCP to public/non-baseline destination (attacker-supplied loc port)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Unauthenticated POST to AIT-BSC /<name>/start with path-traversal form fields (CVE-2026-47731) AIExploitation High
Hunts the actual exploit shape against the AIT-Core BSC HTTP API: POST to /<name>/start carrying attacker-controlled log_dir_path, file_name_pattern, or path form fields with path-traversal indicators (../, %2e%2e, absolute paths like /etc, /home, /root). Pre-patch AIT-Core <3.1.1 and <2.6.1 lets an unauthenticated remote caller use these fields to redirect log_file writes anywhere ait-bsc can write — corruption of .py modules then yields RCE on next restart. Rationale: Targets the exact REST shape from the article (the Bottle route `/<name>/start` registered in `StreamCaptureManagerServer._route()`) plus the three attacker-influenced form fields named in the bug write-up (log_dir_path, file_name_pattern, path) combined with traversal markers (../ %2e%2e absolute /etc /root /home). The article confirms there is no auth on the route and these fields go straight into `os.path.join` without realpath canonicalisation. Cross-checked against the GHSA-p462-prxw-mjx4 advisory and the AIT-Core 3.1.1/2.6.1 patch notes which scope the same parameter list. Falcon FDR doesn't natively ship HTTP request bodies so falcon_logscale_query is empty; the same telemetry is covered by NetworkConnectIP4 in UC2. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p462-prxw-mjx4 • https://github.com/NASA-AMMOS/AIT-Core/releases/tag/3.1.1
ATT&CKT1190 T1565.001
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Burp Pro) probing the BSC endpoint as part of a sanctioned scan
  • Mission-ops engineers running `python_poc.py` from the AIT-Core test harness against a lab BSC instance
  • Custom ground-system tooling that legitimately passes log_dir_path to relocate captures between mission phases
  • Health-check probes that POST malformed bodies to /start to verify the route is alive (yields 400 but trips URL pattern)
Suppression filter
and not (SrcIp in ("10.", "172.16.", "192.168.") and UA has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Tenable","Burp","Acunetix","Nmap")) and not (Uri endswith "/healthcheck/start")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full POST body from the proxy/WAF capture, decode the form fields, and verify whether log_dir_path / path resolves outside the configured `root_log_directory` from bsc.yaml. Pivot on `source IP` to see whether the same caller hit /stats or other handler names. Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter and stop the ait-bsc systemd unit (`systemctl stop ait-bsc`) — do NOT just kill the process because gevent greenlets can keep writing in an infinite-loop bug mentioned in the advisory. Hunt: review DeviceFileEvents for writes by python/ait-bsc into /etc, /root, /home/*/.ssh, site-packages/ait/, or any *.py outside the project tree in the previous 24h; verify SHA256 of any AIT-Core .py against the package wheel hashes; check for outbound TCP from ait-bsc to non-baseline destinations (see related UC2).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionFound","ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python(3(\.\d+)?)?|ait-bsc)(\.exe)?$"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ait-bsc","ait.core.bsc","ait_bsc","StreamCaptureManagerServer","bsc.yaml")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Sessions=count(), AnyLocalPort=any(LocalPort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let TraversalTokens = dynamic(["log_dir_path","file_name_pattern","..%2F","..%2f","..%5C","..%5c","%2e%2e","path=%2F","path=/etc","path=/root","path=/home","path=/var","path=/tmp","log_dir_path=/"]);
let IISHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where csMethod =~ "POST"
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)^/[^/]+/start$"
    | where csUriQuery has_any (TraversalTokens) or csUriStem has_any ("%2e%2e", "..")
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIp=tostring(cIP), DstPort=tostring(sPort), Uri=csUriStem, Detail=csUriQuery, UA=csUserAgent, Source="W3CIIS";
let CEFHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)/[^/]+/start(\?|$)"
    | where Message has_any (TraversalTokens) or RequestURL has_any ("%2e%2e", "..")
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain, DeviceExternalID), SrcIp=SourceIP, DstPort=tostring(DestinationPort), Uri=RequestURL, Detail=Message, UA=RequestClientApplication, Source="CEF";
let SyslogHits = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ProcessName has_any ("ait-bsc","ait_bsc","bsc","python","python3")
    | where SyslogMessage has "/start" and SyslogMessage has_any (TraversalTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIp=HostIP, DstPort="", Uri="/<name>/start", Detail=SyslogMessage, UA="", Source="Syslog";
union IISHits, CEFHits, SyslogHits
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), SampleDetail=any(Detail) by Host, SrcIp, Uri, Source
| order by LastSeen desc
title: AIT-Core BSC Unauthenticated Path-Traversal POST (CVE-2026-47731)
id: 8f3b1a2c-9d4e-4f5a-b6c7-d8e9f0a1b2c3
description: Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-47731 — unauthenticated POST to the AIT-Core Binary Stream Capture /<name>/start endpoint carrying path-traversal-indicative form fields (log_dir_path, file_name_pattern, path) or %2e%2e/../ sequences that redirect the log_file write outside the configured root_log_directory.
references:
    - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p462-prxw-mjx4
author: Threat Hunter Notebooks
date: 2026/06/05
tags:
    - attack.t1190
    - attack.initial_access
    - cve.2026.47731
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection_method:
        cs-method: POST
    selection_uri:
        cs-uri-stem|re: '(?i)^/[^/]+/start$'
    selection_payload:
        cs-uri-query|contains:
            - 'log_dir_path'
            - 'file_name_pattern'
            - '..%2F'
            - '..%2f'
            - '..%5C'
            - '%2e%2e'
            - 'path=%2F'
            - 'path=/etc'
            - 'path=/root'
            - 'path=/home'
            - 'path=/var'
    condition: selection_method and selection_uri and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - Internal pen-test or vuln-scanner traffic (Tenable, Nessus, Burp Suite Pro)

ait-bsc outbound TCP to public/non-baseline destination (attacker-supplied loc port) AICommand & Control High
Detects ait-bsc / python processes running the ait.core.bsc StreamCaptureManager opening outbound TCP/UDP sessions to non-RFC1918, non-baseline destinations. Per CVE-2026-47731 the unauth /<name>/start endpoint lets a remote caller supply arbitrary `loc` + `port` form values which BSC dutifully `gevent.spawn`s a socket against — making BSC initiate egress to attacker-controlled infrastructure that then streams attacker-chosen bytes back into the file append sink. Rationale: Anchors directly on the article-confirmed primitive: the attacker controls `loc` and `port` in the form body and BSC `gevent.spawn`s a SocketStreamCapturer at that endpoint — i.e. BSC initiates the egress under attacker direction. Process-context match uses the exact module path (`ait.core.bsc`), class name (`StreamCaptureManagerServer`), and config file (`bsc.yaml`) shown in the source excerpt. Sentinel query splits process-context resolution onto ImProcessCreate (which carries ActingProcessCommandLine) and joins by DvcHostname into ImNetworkSession (which does not) — the schema-correct way to express the same logic the Defender query expresses inline. Cross-checked against GHSA-p462-prxw-mjx4 patch diff which restricts socket creation to validated paths only. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p462-prxw-mjx4 • https://github.com/NASA-AMMOS/AIT-Core/blob/main/ait/core/bsc.py
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1659
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ground-station configurations where BSC connects to a public-IP downlink receiver (rare, but check bsc.yaml first)
  • Mission-ops sites running ait-bsc against a cloud-hosted relay (AWS Ground Station, Azure Orbital) which presents as a public IP
  • Engineer testing against a remote development BSC server over a tunnel that egresses to the tunnel endpoint's public IP
  • Updates / pip installs run from the same venv where ait-bsc is installed (mitigated by the process-name filter, but pip can shell into python entrypoints)
Suppression filter
| where not (DstIpAddr in ("<known_ground_station_ip_1>","<known_ground_station_ip_2>")) and not (DstPortNumber in (8080, 8443) and BscCommandLine has "--allow-public-relay")
Response runbook
Triage: pull bsc.yaml from the host and confirm the destination IP+port is NOT in the configured handler list — any unrecognised loc is high-fidelity evil. Capture the BSC handler stats endpoint output (`GET /stats`) to enumerate every currently registered logger and their loc/port/path. Contain: stop the ait-bsc service and revoke any open TCP socket — note the advisory warns of an infinite-loop write bug on close, so plan disk-space monitoring during teardown. Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for writes by the same ait-bsc PID within the same window, especially to .py / .sh / authorized_keys / cron paths; verify all AIT-Core site-packages files match the wheel hash; pivot the remote IP across DNS / proxy logs to find other internal hosts that reached out to it.

Securing CI/CD in an agentic world: Claude Code Github action case

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-05 7 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a prompt injection pathway in Claude Code GitHub Action that allowed access to workflow secrets under specific conditions. This research examines the attack chain, responsible disclosure process, Anthropic's mitigation, and guidance for securing AI-powered CI/CD workflows. The post Securing CI/CD in an agentic world: Claude Code Github action case appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Claude Code Action Read tool exfil: node opens /proc/<pid>/environ on Linux CI runner · [LLM] Claude Code Read tool steered to cloud-credential files on GitHub Actions runner · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GitHub Actions runner: node from Claude Code Action egresses to non-Anthropic/non-GitHub endpoint
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Claude Code Action Read tool exfil: node opens /proc/<pid>/environ on Linux CI runner AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact exploitation primitive Microsoft Threat Intelligence described: the Claude Code Action's in-process Read tool, when steered by an injected prompt, opens /proc/self/environ (or /proc/<pid>/environ) to harvest the workflow's ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN, and OIDC credentials. Pre-fix (claude-code-action <2.1.128) the Bubblewrap sandbox + CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB does not cover Read, so the node process serving Claude Code opens /proc directly — a path almost nothing legitimate touches on a build runner. Rationale: Article names the exact primitive: 'eventually authorized to access /proc/self/environ, reading the workflow's ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'. We pin on the Linux file path regex + node as the actor. The Read tool runs in-process inside node (not via Bash), so the file event is the only signal — there is no child process to pivot on. Corroborated by Flatt Security (flatt.tech) and Hacker News reporting which describe the same /proc/self/environ exfil chain. Cross-checked against: • https://flatt.tech/research/posts/poisoning-claude-code-one-github-issue-to-break-the-supply-chain/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/claude-code-github-action-flaw-let-one.html • https://oddguan.com/blog/comment-and-control-prompt-injection-credential-theft-claude-code-gemini-cli-github-copilot/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1212 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container/process observability agents (datadog-agent, sysdig, falcon-sensor, osquery) using a bundled node helper to enumerate process env for inventory
  • Self-hosted runner image pre-flight scripts that introspect node's own environment for diagnostics (e.g. Node's --inspect tooling)
  • node-based Kubernetes operators (kube-state-metrics ports, Pulumi/CDK preview scripts) iterating /proc to map sibling containers
  • Security tooling that legitimately scans /proc for secret leakage (gitleaks/trufflehog wrapper jobs)
  • Node debugger sessions where a developer manually reads /proc/self/environ to diagnose env-var passing
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("datadog-agent", "sysdig", "falcon-sensor", "osqueryd", "trufflehog", "gitleaks")) and not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/opt/datadog-agent" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/opt/sysdig")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and folder path — confirm node was launched from `_actions/anthropics/claude-code-action*` or `@anthropic-ai/claude-code`. Pull the GitHub run ID from the runner work dir (`/home/runner/work/<repo>/<repo>` or env GITHUB_RUN_ID) and fetch the triggering issue/PR body via gh api; look for HTML-comment payloads, /proc references, or Read-tool instructions. Step 2 (contain): Rotate ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN scopes, any OIDC-issued cloud creds, and every other secret exposed to that job. Disable the workflow file until upgraded to claude-code-action ≥2.1.128. For self-hosted runners, isolate the runner host pending forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same node PID to DeviceNetworkEvents/NetworkConnectIP4 in the surrounding 60s for outbound to non-Anthropic/non-GitHub IPs (exfil destination). Hunt repo-wide for other workflows pinning vulnerable claude-code-action SHAs. Audit recent PRs opened by the AI bot accoun
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node"
| where FolderPath matches regex @"^/proc/(self|\d+)/environ$"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("_work/", "actions-runner", "_actions/anthropics/claude-code-action", "runners/") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@anthropic-ai/claude-code", "claude-code-action")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/node" or ActingProcessName =~ "node"
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"^/proc/(self|\d+)/environ$"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("claude-code", "@anthropic-ai", "_actions/anthropics", "actions-runner", "/_work/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId, TargetFilePath, EventType, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  condition: selection_proc and selection_path

  - Process inspection / observability agents (e.g. Datadog process-agent, sysdig) running as node
  - Self-introspection by a Node tool reading its OWN /proc/self/environ for debugging (rare in CI)

Claude Code Read tool steered to cloud-credential files on GitHub Actions runner AIExploitation Medium
Even after the /proc fix in claude-code-action 2.1.128, an attacker who controls the prompt can still steer the Read tool to any path the runner can see. This hunts node — running from the Actions work dir — opening the common secret stores a CI job tends to have on disk: ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc (NPM publish token), ~/.docker/config.json (registry token), ~/.kube/config, ~/.netrc, SSH keys, .env files. Microsoft's article explicitly calls out that 'once an attacker can influence the agent, they might be able to steer it toward sensitive files available inside the CI runner environment'. Rationale: Article: 'once an attacker can influence the agent, they might be able to steer it toward sensitive files available inside the CI runner environment.' We restrict to node spawned from `_work/` or the anthropic action checkout dir so legit user shell activity reading `~/.aws/credentials` doesn't fire. Path list is the GitHub Actions secret canon — npm publish tokens, docker registry creds, GitHub CLI tokens, terraform/pypi publishers — all of which routinely live in runner home dirs. Cross-checked: Flatt's writeup confirms ANTHROPIC_API_KEY + GITHUB_TOKEN + OIDC creds are the named targets, the broader hunt covers what would be next. Cross-checked against: • https://flatt.tech/research/posts/poisoning-claude-code-one-github-issue-to-break-the-supply-chain/ • https://oddguan.com/blog/comment-and-control-prompt-injection-credential-theft-claude-code-gemini-cli-github-copilot/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1078.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate `npm publish` step in CI reading ~/.npmrc — node IS the actor, and the file IS a token store
  • AWS CDK / Pulumi / terraform-cdk preview steps where node reads ~/.aws/credentials via the AWS SDK
  • `docker login` wrapper jobs invoking a node-based credential helper that reads ~/.docker/config.json
  • GitHub CLI integration tests that invoke `gh` from node and read ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml
  • Self-hosted runner provisioning script (Ansible/Chef) using node-based tasks to template .env / .npmrc
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish", "yarn publish", "docker login", "terraform apply", "terraform plan", "cdk deploy", "cdk synth", "pulumi up", "pulumi preview", "gh auth", "actions/setup-node"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Map the node PID to the GitHub Actions run — InitiatingProcessFolderPath under `_actions/anthropics/claude-code-action*` is the smoking gun. Fetch the triggering issue/PR/comment via `gh api` and look for prompt-injection markers (HTML comments, 'read the file', '/proc/', 'cat ~/.aws'). Validate whether the build step has a legitimate reason to read the file (npm publish, terraform apply). Step 2 (contain): If injection confirmed, rotate every secret the file held (NPM token, AWS keys, kube token, etc.) plus every other secret in the workflow's environment — the agent had broad Read access. Pause the workflow until upgraded past claude-code-action 2.1.128 AND tool-permission scope is reviewed. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep DeviceFileEvents/ImFileEvent for the same node PID reading additional paths in the 5 min before/after; pull DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound from the same PID; query GitHub audit log for any commits/PRs the bot account created in the same window — Microsoft's
let CredPaths = dynamic([".aws/credentials", ".npmrc", ".gitconfig", ".docker/config.json", ".kube/config", ".netrc", "/.env", ".config/gh/hosts.yml", ".terraformrc", ".pypirc"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("_work/", "actions-runner", "_actions/anthropics/claude-code-action") 
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@anthropic-ai/claude-code", "claude-code-action")
| where FolderPath has_any (CredPaths)
   or FolderPath matches regex @"\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|dsa|ecdsa)$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let CredPaths = dynamic([".aws/credentials", ".npmrc", ".gitconfig", ".docker/config.json", ".kube/config", ".netrc", "/.env", ".config/gh/hosts.yml", ".terraformrc", ".pypirc"]);
ImFileEvent

| where ActingProcessName endswith "/node" or ActingProcessName =~ "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("claude-code", "@anthropic-ai", "_actions/anthropics", "/_work/", "actions-runner")

| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Claude Code Read Tool Accessing Credential Files on GitHub Actions Runner
id: b2c3d4e5-f6a7-4890-9bcd-ef0123456789
description: Node.js (running Claude Code Action or the Anthropic SDK) opening common credential / token files on a Linux GitHub Actions runner. Catches Read-tool abuse beyond the patched /proc primitive — an attacker who controls the AI prompt can still steer Read at ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json, SSH keys, and .env.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/05/securing-ci-cd-in-agentic-world-claude-code-github-action-case/
  - https://flatt.tech/research/posts/poisoning-claude-code-one-github-issue-to-break-the-supply-chain/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/05
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1552.004
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith: '/node'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/.aws/credentials'
      - '/.npmrc'
      - '/.gitconfig'
      - '/.docker/config.json'
      - '/.kube/config'
      - '/.netrc'
      - '/.config/gh/hosts.yml'
      - '/.terraformrc'

    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '/.env'
  selection_ssh:
    TargetFilename|re: '/\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|dsa|ecdsa)$'

falsepositives:
  - Genuine CI jobs that legitimately use these credentials (build step reading .npmrc to publish, terraform reading .aws/credentials). Refine by parent-process / runner identity.
level: high
